extracted.intended_audience: AP English Literature and Composition exam readers, teachers, and students preparing for the AP free-response section
extracted.subtask_description: Scoring guidelines for AP English Literature free-response essays (prose-fiction analysis and literary argument), defining point-by-point criteria for thesis, evidence/commentary, and sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row A — Thesis (Q2 Prose Fiction Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation. (0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 0 points: No defensible thesis; thesis only restates the prompt; provides a summary with no coherent claim; thesis that does not respond to the prompt. 1 point: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation. Additional notes: The thesis may be more than one sentence (sentences must be in close proximity). The thesis may be anywhere within the response. For a thesis to be defensible, the passage must include at least minimal evidence that could be used to support that thesis (the student need not cite that evidence to earn the thesis point). The thesis may establish a line of reasoning that structures the essay, but it needn’t do so to earn the thesis point. A thesis that meets the criteria can be awarded the point whether or not the rest of the response successfully supports that line of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row B — Evidence AND Commentary (Q2 Prose Fiction Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures the quality of evidence and commentary supporting the argument (0–4 points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring breakdown: 0 points — Simply restates thesis (if present), repeats provided information, or offers information irrelevant to the prompt. 1 point — EVIDENCE: Provides evidence that is mostly general. (COMMENTARY: Summarizes the evidence but does not explain how the evidence supports the student’s argument.) 2 points — EVIDENCE: Provides some specific, relevant evidence. (COMMENTARY: Explains how some of the evidence relates to the student’s argument, but no line of reasoning is established, or the line of reasoning is faulty.) 3 points — EVIDENCE: Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning. (COMMENTARY: Explains how some of the evidence supports a line of reasoning.) 4 points — EVIDENCE: Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning. (COMMENTARY: Consistently explains how the evidence supports a line of reasoning and explains how multiple literary elements or techniques in the passage contribute to its meaning.) Decision rules/typical responses: 1-point responses tend to focus on broad narrative developments or description rather than specific details/techniques; 2-point responses mix specific evidence and generalities and may have simplistic or repetitive explanations; 3-point responses uniformly offer evidence to support claims and organize an argument as a line of reasoning; 4-point responses uniformly offer specific details to build interpretation and organize multiple supporting claims each with adequate evidence clearly explained. Additional notes: Writing that suffers grammatical/mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the fourth point in this row. To earn the fourth point, the response may observe multiple instances of the same literary element/technique if each instance further contributes to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row C — Sophistication (Q2 Prose Fiction Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assesses whether the response demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument (0–1 points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 0 points: Does not meet the criteria for one point. Responses that do not earn this point include those that attempt to contextualize but rely on sweeping generalizations, only hint at alternative interpretations, oversimplify complexities, or use complex language ineffectively. 1 point: Demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument. Ways to earn this point include: identifying and exploring complexities or tensions within the passage; illuminating interpretation by situating it within a broader context; accounting for alternative interpretations; employing a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive. Additional note: This point should be awarded only if the sophistication or complex understanding is part of the student’s argument, not merely a phrase or reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row A — Thesis (Q3 Literary Argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the selected work. (0-1 points)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 0 points: No defensible thesis; restates the prompt; makes generalized comments about the selected work that don’t respond to the prompt; provides a summary with no coherent claim. 1 point: Provides a defensible interpretation of how a character responds to a hierarchy in the selected work OR makes a claim about how that response contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. Additional notes: The thesis may be more than one sentence (sentences must be in close proximity). The thesis may be anywhere in the response. For a thesis to be defensible, the selected work must include at least minimal evidence that could be used to support that thesis (student need not cite that evidence). Any reasonable interpretation of “hierarchical structure” is acceptable. A thesis that meets the criteria can earn the point regardless of whether the rest of the response supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row B — Evidence AND Commentary (Q3 Literary Argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluates evidence from the selected work and the quality of commentary linking evidence to the argument (0–4 points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring breakdown: 0 points — Simply restates thesis, repeats provided information, or offers information irrelevant to the prompt. 1 point — EVIDENCE: Provides evidence that is mostly general. (COMMENTARY: Summarizes the evidence but does not explain how the evidence supports the argument.) 2 points — EVIDENCE: Provides some specific, relevant evidence. (COMMENTARY: Explains how some of the evidence relates to the argument, but no clear line of reasoning is established or the line is faulty.) 3 points — EVIDENCE: Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning. (COMMENTARY: Explains how some of the evidence supports a line of reasoning.) 4 points — EVIDENCE: Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning. (COMMENTARY: Consistently explains how the evidence supports a line of reasoning; to earn the fourth point, the response must address the interpretation of the selected work as a whole.) Decision rules/typical responses: 1-point responses focus on overarching narrative rather than specific details; 2-point responses mix specific evidence and broad generalities and may fail to explain progression of claims; 3-point responses uniformly offer evidence and build a line of reasoning composed of multiple supporting claims; 4-point responses focus on specific details to build interpretation and support multiple claims with adequate evidence explained. Additional notes: Writing with grammatical/mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the fourth point in this row.

rubrics_metrics.name: Row C — Sophistication (Q3 Literary Argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determines whether the response demonstrates sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument about the selected work (0–1 points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 0 points: Does not meet criteria — attempts that are predominantly sweeping generalizations, only hint at other interpretations, oversimplify complexities, or use ineffective complex language will not earn the point. 1 point: Demonstrates sophistication by doing any of the following: identifying and exploring complexities or tensions within the selected work; illuminating interpretation by situating it within a broader context; accounting for alternative interpretations; employing a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive. Additional note: Award this point only if the sophistication or complex understanding is integral to the student’s argument, not just a phrase or reference.
